171.event_title: The fall and Siberian exile of Prince Menshikov
171.place: St Petersburg and Berezov (Beryozovo), Siberia, Russia
171.event: Aleksandr Menshikov, Peter the Great's closest associate, had been under almost continuous investigation for corrupt practices while helping to run the state, and after the death of Catherine I he was accused of abuses and embezzlement of state property. In September 1727 a decree of the young Emperor Peter II stripped him of all his offices, honours, titles and property, and he was exiled with his family to Berezov in Siberia. His wife died on the journey, a daughter died in exile in 1728, and Menshikov himself died there in 1729.
171.explanation: The most powerful man in Russia lost everything at a stroke, and his household shared his ruin.
171.tie_back: The kural warns that coveting what belongs to others brings ruin on one's family and guilt on oneself, and Menshikov's grasping at state wealth ended with his whole family in exile.
171._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of ruin falling on the coveter's family, though court rivals such as the Dolgorukys also engineered his fall.

172.event_title: The insulin team sells its patent to the University of Toronto for one dollar each
172.event: After Frederick Banting, Charles Best, James Collip and their colleagues developed insulin at the University of Toronto, Banting objected to taking out patents and charging royalties for its manufacture. Banting, Best and Collip assigned their patent rights on insulin and its method of preparation to the University of Toronto for one dollar each, so that no one could secure a profitable private monopoly. The university then licensed manufacturers and used the royalties to fund further research.
172.explanation: The discoverers of a life-saving drug could have grown rich from it but chose to place it in public trust.
172.tie_back: The kural says those who feel shame at unfairness will not do disgraceful things for gain, and the insulin team refused to profit privately from the suffering of diabetic patients.
172._accuracy_note: A strong example of refusing ill-fitting profit, though patenting itself is not disgraceful and the kural is aimed at gain taken from others.

173.event_title: Bobby Jones calls a penalty on himself at the U.S. Open
173.place: Worcester Country Club, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States
173.event: During the first round of the 1925 U.S. Open, the amateur golfer Bobby Jones's club moved his ball slightly as he addressed it on the 11th hole. No official, playing partner or spectator saw it, but Jones reported it and took a one-stroke penalty. He finished the 72 holes tied with Willie Macfarlane and lost the title in a playoff.
173.explanation: Jones gave up a national championship rather than take an advantage no one else would have known about, and his integrity became part of golf's tradition.
173.tie_back: The kural says those who seek lasting joy will not do wrong for a small passing gain, and Jones preferred his honour to a title won unfairly.
173._accuracy_note: A clear case of refusing a small unfair gain for a lasting good, though it concerns honesty in sport rather than coveting another's property.

174.event_title: Thomas Paine gives up the profits of Common Sense
174.event: Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense, published in January 1776, sold in enormous numbers and helped turn American opinion toward independence. Paine declined royalties after the first printing so that the pamphlet could be sold cheaply and reprinted freely, and gave his profits to buy mittens for Continental troops. By the end of the Revolution he was penniless and had to ask Congress for reimbursement of his expenses.
174.explanation: Paine, a man of modest means, chose not to enrich himself from the most successful publication of the age.
174.tie_back: The kural says the self-mastered do not covet others' wealth even when they think themselves poor, and Paine stayed poor rather than take wealth from his cause.
174._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Paine declined his own earnings rather than resisting the temptation to take another's property.

175.event_title: The arrest of Nicolas Fouquet after the fete at Vaux-le-Vicomte
175.event: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's superintendent of finances and a cultivated patron of writers and artists, built the magnificent chateau of Vaux-le-Vicomte and entertained the king there with a lavish fete on 17 August 1661. On 5 September 1661 he was arrested at Nantes by d'Artagnan and charged with embezzlement of public funds. After a trial lasting about three years the judges voted for banishment, but the king changed the sentence to life imprisonment, and Fouquet died in the fortress of Pignerol in 1680.
175.explanation: One of the most brilliant and refined men in France ended his life in prison because of the way he had enriched himself from state funds.
175.tie_back: The kural asks what use a subtle and broad mind is if its owner covets others' goods, and Fouquet's taste and talent could not save him once he was charged with taking public money.
175._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for brilliance undone by greed, though the king's suspicion and Colbert's rivalry also drove the prosecution.

176.event_title: Televangelist Jim Bakker is convicted of fraud
176.event: Jim Bakker built the PTL television ministry into a large religious enterprise that included the Heritage USA resort in South Carolina. Prosecutors showed that he had sold far more lifetime partnerships, promising yearly lodging at the resort, than could ever be honoured, and diverted the money to other uses. In October 1989 a federal jury convicted him on all 24 counts of fraud and conspiracy, and he was sentenced to 45 years in prison, later reduced; he served almost five years.
176.explanation: A preacher who had led a large ministry lost his ministry, his freedom and his reputation through greed for his followers' money.
176.tie_back: The kural says even one who has stood on the path of virtue and grace will be ruined if he covets others' wealth, and Bakker's fall from ministry to prison shows exactly that.
176._accuracy_note: Close to a dramatisation of the kural: a religious leader ruined by plotting to take the money of others.

177.event_title: Cicero prosecutes Verres for plundering Sicily
177.event: Gaius Verres, Roman governor of Sicily from 73 to 71 BCE, exploited the province ruthlessly, seizing money and art from its people. The Sicilians asked Cicero to prosecute him, and in 70 BCE Cicero gathered evidence across the island and opened the case with such force that Verres' defender, Hortensius, abandoned the defence. Before the hearing of evidence was over, Verres left Rome for exile in Massilia (Marseille), was condemned in his absence, and spent the rest of his life in exile.
177.explanation: The fortune Verres extracted from Sicily brought him not enjoyment but disgrace and a lifetime of exile, and Cicero's speeches made his name a byword for corruption.
177.tie_back: The kural warns that wealth gained by coveting seldom bears good fruit when it ripens, and Verres' plunder ripened into ruin and exile.
177._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of ill-gotten wealth turning to ruin, though Verres reportedly kept part of his fortune in exile.

178.event_title: The failure of the Darien scheme
178.place: Darien, Isthmus of Panama, and Scotland
178.event: Between 1698 and 1700 the Company of Scotland sent expeditions to found a Scottish colony and trading centre at Darien on the Isthmus of Panama, a region claimed by Spain. The venture collapsed amid disease, Spanish resistance and lack of English support, costing about 2,000 lives. National Museums Scotland estimates that Scotland lost a quarter of its liquid capital, and the National Library of Scotland notes that the loss is thought to have hastened the Union with England in 1707.
178.explanation: A nation staked a large share of its wealth on seizing a foothold in land others claimed, and the loss shook its economy and independence.
178.tie_back: The kural says the way to keep one's wealth from dwindling is not to covet what is in another's hands, and Scotland's grab for Spanish-claimed land drained its wealth instead.
178._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the scheme was a trade venture as much as a grab for others' land, so the fit to coveting is partial.

179.event_title: American women give Marie Curie a gram of radium
179.place: The White House, Washington, D.C., United States
179.event: Marie Curie had deliberately chosen not to patent radium or its medical uses, and by 1920 its high price left her without enough for her own research in Paris. The journalist Marie Meloney organised a fund among American women that raised the money to buy a gram of radium for her. On 20 May 1921 President Warren G. Harding presented the gift to Curie at the White House on behalf of the women of America.
179.explanation: Curie had refused to profit from her discovery, and the resources she needed came to her unasked through the gratitude of others.
179.tie_back: The kural says fortune recognises the worth of those who do not covet and seeks them out of her own accord, and the radium Curie would not profit from came to her as a gift.
179._accuracy_note: Close to a dramatisation of the kural: one who declined to grasp at wealth was sought out by it.

180.event_title: The Athenian expedition to Sicily ends in disaster
180.event: In 415 BCE Athens, answering an appeal from Segesta and hoping to extend its power over Sicily, sent a great fleet and army against Syracuse, over the objections of the general Nicias. Syracuse, reinforced by Sparta and Corinth, held out, and in 413 BCE the Athenians lost the decisive naval battle in the harbour of Syracuse. The retreating army surrendered, the generals Nicias and Demosthenes were executed, and Thucydides records that at least 7,000 prisoners were taken.
180.explanation: Thucydides presents the expedition as an overreach by a city that wanted more than it needed, and its failure was a turning point toward Athens' defeat in the Peloponnesian War.
180.tie_back: The kural says coveting without weighing the consequences gives birth to destruction, and Athens' reach for Sicily ended in the loss of its fleet and army.
180._accuracy_note: Strongly illustrates the first half of the kural; the second half, victory born of non-desire, is not shown.
